text.hook:
malloc's fast path takes tens of nanoseconds.
So why do low-latency systems still write memory pools?

Here is the mental model, plus 6 myths that fail interviews. Save it. 💡
text.body:
Inside:
1. What a pool exploits
2. Designing a fixed-size pool
3. The exhaustion policy
4. std::pmr resources and their traps
5. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

slides.hero:
Memory pools
& std::pmr:
the mental model
+ 6 myths
slides.lead: Why pools exist, how to design one, and the pmr rules that surprise people.

slides.title: A pool exploits what you know

cards.label: Fixed size
cards.text: One type (orders, messages): a fixed-size pool with a free list.

cards.label: Grouped lifetime
cards.text: Everything for one request dies together: an arena, freed in one step.

cards.label: Known thread
cards.text: One thread allocates and frees: no synchronization at all.

slides.takeaway: The win is **predictability** (tail latency), not a faster average. Measure both.

slides.title: Storage once, objects many times
steps: Startup: one raw, aligned block for N slots. Not `new T[N]`: that runs N constructors.
Free slots form an intrusive list: each stores the next pointer in its own bytes.
Acquire: pop the head, placement new. Constructor throws? Push the slot back.
Release: `~T()`, push the slot. Never `delete p`. Hand out `unique_ptr<T, PoolDeleter>`.

slides.title: All slots in use. Now what?
rows: Telemetry, or data a snapshot replaces
Only if it shows in metrics
slides.takeaway: Size from measured peak + headroom, export the high-water mark, pre-fault the pages at startup.

slides.title: The standard memory resources
slides.takeaway: Resources chain through an upstream. `null_memory_resource()` as upstream turns a buffer into a hard bound.

slides.hero:
One shared free list
is one hot
cache line.
slides.lead: Usual answer: per-thread pools. A cross-thread free goes back through a queue or a remote-free list.

slides.title: Where pmr surprises people
items: The resource must outlive its containers: declare it first
Move-assign across different resources: element-wise, O(n), allocates
slides.takeaway: Decide the resource at construction and pass it explicitly. Assignment never moves data into an arena.

items.truth: Its main value is bounded, predictable cost. Measure average and tail separately.

items.myth: "`new T[N]` is a good way to create the pool's storage."
items.truth: It runs N constructors. A pool needs raw aligned storage and constructs on acquire.
Run the destructor and return the slot. The storage belongs to the pool.

items.myth: "A monotonic resource over a 4096-byte buffer never touches the heap."
items.truth: When the buffer runs out it asks its upstream: the heap, unless that is `null_memory_resource()`.
It does not exist. Use `unsynchronized_pool_resource` or `synchronized_pool_resource`.

items.myth: "A pool freeing a block returns memory to the OS."
items.truth: The block goes back to the pool. Chunks return only on `release()` or destruction.

slides.hero:
Pools trade generality
for predictability.

pmr: choose the resource
at construction.
slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
The loader builds a vector in a fast local arena and returns it by value.
Move semantics make that safe, right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: It looks like textbook modern C++. Read it the way a reviewer would.

slides.title: What does `main` print?

slides.verdict_sub: Here (GCC 11, -O0): a stale `99` on a terminal, then a segfault. ASan: heap-use-after-free on `v[99]`
bullets: `return v;` moves (or elides) the vector. A moved pmr vector keeps the **source's** resource.
So the returned `v` still points into `arena`'s chunks and holds `&arena`.
`arena` dies at the end of `load()` and frees every chunk.
`v[99]` reads freed memory; `v`'s destructor then calls a dead resource.

slides.title: The caller owns the resource
slides.takeaway: A pmr container stores a raw `memory_resource*`. It never owns the resource: the resource must outlive it.

text.hook:
One arena-backed vector, passed by value twice: once copied, once moved.
Which call still uses the arena?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Same function, same vector, two calls. The only difference is std::move.

slides.title: What does this print?

slides.verdict_sub: Copy construction drops the arena. Move construction keeps it.
bullets: pmr copy construction uses `select_on_container_copy_construction()`: a default allocator, so the default resource (normally the heap).
Call 2 move-constructs: the parameter takes the source's resource, `arena`.
Copy **assignment** differs again: the target keeps its own resource.
slides.wrong: "1, then 1: a copy keeps the resource"

slides.title: Never leave the arena by accident
slides.takeaway: Hidden copies (by-value parameters, `auto x = member;`) silently move data to the heap.

text.hook:
Allocate 64 bytes from an arena. Free them. Allocate 64 again.
Surely you get the same block back?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Pick this resource for the wrong workload and memory grows without bound.

slides.title: What does it print?

slides.verdict_sub: `deallocate` does nothing: it is an arena
bullets: Allocate = align + bump a pointer. When full, ask upstream for a bigger chunk.
No per-block free list or merging: that is why allocation is so cheap.
Memory comes back only on `release()` or destruction, all at once.
A free list is a pool resource (`unsynchronized_pool_resource`).
slides.wrong: "A freed block is reused by the next allocation"

slides.title: One arena per unit of work
bullets: Harmful: independent lifetimes, growing or churning containers.
slides.takeaway: Monotonic = bump allocate, never free individually, release everything together.

text.hook:
The vector lives in your arena. You push one 100-char string.
How many times does it touch the global heap?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: A favourite pmr follow-up in low-latency interviews.

slides.title: What does it print? (GCC/libstdc++)

slides.verdict_sub: Only the vector's own array comes from `arena`
bullets: `std::string` uses `std::allocator`: its 100 chars go to the global heap.
SSO holds only short strings (15 chars in libstdc++).
It compiles: a `pmr::vector` can hold any element type.
Short strings in tests hide it: they allocate nothing at all.
slides.wrong: "Once the outer container is pmr, everything inside is in the arena"

slides.title: pmr all the way down
bullets: The vector passes `arena` to each `pmr::string`: uses-allocator construction.
slides.takeaway: Use pmr types all the way down, and prove where allocations go with a counting resource in tests.
